# IEEE Transactions on Multimedia 2026 | ULightIF

ULightIF: Unsupervised Low Light Infrared and Visible Image Fusion Method

## 🙌 1 Introduction

  * This is the official implementation of our paper titled "ULightIF: Unsupervised Low Light Infrared and Visible Image Fusion Method". This paper has been accepted by IEEE Transactions on Multimedia.
  * If you have any question about this code, feel free to reach me(cmuhang@163.com)

## 🌐 2 Prepare Your Dataset

Please download the datasets from the following links: MSRS | LLVIP | M3FD.

Download the corresponding datasets following their official instructions, and then modify the dataset paths in the `options.py` configuration file.

## 🛠️ 3 Pretrained Weights

The weight files released in the `weights` directory are the original paper checkpoints used by `test_p.py`.

## 🚀 4 Usage

To facilitate the open-source release, we refactored the codebase using PyTorch Lightning, improving readability and maintainability. Accordingly, this repository provides two testing scripts:

  * `test_p.py`: reproduces the results in the paper.
  * `test.py`: evaluates models trained with the refactored training pipeline.

Users may select either the intermediate fusion result or the final enhanced result for comparison, depending on whether the task targets standard or low-light image fusion.

### 📖 4.1 Training

Before training, please download and prepare the dataset and configure the training settings in `options.py`. Then run:
    
    python train.py

### 🧩 4.2 Testing

To reproduce the results reported in the paper, run:
    
    python test_p.py

To test your own trained model, run:
    
    python test.py

## Abstract:

Current advanced research on infrared and visible image fusion (IVIF) primarily focuses on improving fusion performance under normal illumination, while its applicability in low-light conditions remains underexplored. To address this, we propose ULightIF, an unsupervised IVIF framework tailored for low-light scenarios. Our method innovatively leverages the pre-enhanced results from the “enhance first, fuse later” process to guide the “fuse first, enhance later” procedure, thereby overcoming the limitations of existing low-light fusion methods that typically rely on a single strategy. From a structural perspective, ULightIF integrates low-light enhancement, multimodal image fusion, and image decomposition subnetworks within a flexible architecture. It further adopts a convolutional re-parameterization technique, resulting in a lightweight network with only approximately 0.0597M parameters. The network is trained using a carefully designed set of unsupervised loss functions, using only paired low-light infrared and visible images without requiring normally illuminated data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves a favorable balance between high-quality visual performance and adaptability to downstream tasks, while maintaining high efficiency for practical deployment.

##### Summary

Current advanced research on infrared and visible image fusion (IVIF) primarily focuses on improving fusion performance under normal illumination, while its applicability in low-light conditions remains underexplored. To address this, we propose ULightIF, an unsupervised IVIF framework tailored for low-light scenarios. Our method innovatively leverages the pre-enhanced results from the "enhance first, fuse later" process to guide the "fuse first, enhance later" procedure, thereby overcoming the limitations of existing low-light fusion methods that typically rely on a single strategy. From a structural perspective, ULightIF integrates low-light enhancement, multimodal image fusion, and image decomposition subnetworks within a flexible architecture. It further adopts a convolutional re-parameterization technique, resulting in a lightweight network with only approximately 0.0597M parameters. The network is trained using a carefully designed set of unsupervised loss functions, using only paired low-light infrared and visible images without requiring normally illuminated data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves a favorable balance between high-quality visual performance and adaptability to downstream tasks, while maintaining high efficiency for practical deployment.
